strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: the paper clearly identifies a real limitation of existing open-set/open-vocabulary VAD methods (fixed anomaly definitions) and formalizes it as a concept-drift issue with a clean probabilistic framing (P(Y|V,Z)), which gives the paradigm shift theoretical grounding rather than being purely heuristic.

New large-scale dataset (PreVAD) with 35,279 videos, multi-level taxonomy (7 first-level, 35 sub-categories), and free-form anomaly descriptions, which is substantially larger and more diverse than prior VAD datasets and independent from existing VAD benchmark sources (enabling genuine cross-dataset zero-shot evaluation without data leakage).

Extensive zero-shot evaluation across seven diverse datasets (UCF-Crime, XD-Violence, MSAD, UBNormal, DoTA, TAD, LAD) is much broader than prior work, which typically evaluates on 1-2 datasets, strengthening claims of open-world generalization.

Reasonable ablations disentangling the effects of dataset scale, architecture, and each proposed component (dynamic video synthesis, negative mining, language guidance), showing each contributes incrementally to performance.

Qualitative case studies (Fig. 7) directly illustrate the core claimed capability (adapting to redefinition of anomaly categories at inference time) in a way competitor methods cannot, which is a compelling and intuitive demonstration of the paradigm's practical value.
The scalable, semi-automated data curation pipeline (MLLM-based annotation/verification) is a practical contribution that could be reused/extended by the community, given release plans.
weaknesses: The dataset construction pipeline (MLLM-generated descriptions, MLLM/VLM verified consistency, LLM anomaly confirmation) has no reported human validation study measuring accuracy/quality of automated annotations (e.g., agreement between MLLM outputs and human judgment, error rates), so the actual annotation quality and label noise level of PreVAD remain unverified beyond a single qualitative example.

Classification F1 results in Table 3 show LaGoVAD trained on PreVAD underperforms VadCLIP trained on PreVAD on UCF-Crime F1 (16.64 vs 17.81), which is not discussed or explained, raising questions about consistency of the claimed 'comprehensive improvements'.

The core quantitative demonstration of concept-drift adaptability (Section 6.4/Fig. 7) is only qualitative/anecdotal (two hand-picked examples); there is no quantitative benchmark or metric that measures how well the model handles definition changes at scale (e.g., systematically varying definitions and measuring detection accuracy shifts across many categories), which is the paper's central novel claim.

Baselines for the new paradigm are limited to re-purposed weakly-supervised/open-vocabulary methods (PEL, VadCLIP, OVVAD) that were never designed for user-defined language conditioning at test time; there is no comparison against a more natural baseline such as a strong multimodal LLM prompted zero-shot with the same textual definitions, which would better contextualize how much of the gain comes from the paradigm versus from the larger/more diverse training data.

The paper's central formal justification (Eq. 1-4) is somewhat informal: the claim 'we hypothesize Y is solely determined by Z and V' is an assumption not empirically validated, and the argument that conditioning on Z 'avoids' concept drift is more of a reframing (the drift is pushed into modeling P(Z|V) or requires the user to correctly specify Z) rather than a proven solution to the underlying learning problem.

Reproducibility depends on release of code, data, and detailed MLLM prompting recipes; while promised, at submission time these are not verifiable, and details of the automated pipeline (specific MLLM/VLM/LLM models, prompts, thresholds) are deferred entirely to supplementary material not included here.

Given the dataset is sourced substantially from existing video-text datasets (57%) and web/streaming (43%), there could be latent overlap in underlying video content/domains with some of the seven zero-shot evaluation datasets (e.g., crime/traffic scenes commonly sourced from YouTube), and the paper does not report a deduplication or overlap analysis against the test benchmarks, raising some risk of inflated zero-shot numbers.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and underexplored problem: that anomaly definitions can shift across users/contexts (concept drift), and formalizes it via a clean probabilistic decomposition P(Y|V) = sum_z P(Y|V,Z)P(Z|V).

PreVAD is a large-scale (35,279 videos) and diverse dataset with hierarchical taxonomy (7 top-level, 35 sub-categories) and free-form anomaly descriptions, which is a genuinely useful resource if released as promised.

Extensive zero-shot evaluation across seven established VAD benchmarks (UCF-Crime, XD-Violence, MSAD, UBNormal, DoTA, TAD, LAD) shows consistent numerical improvements over several strong baselines (PEL, VadCLIP, LAVAD, MultiDomain, OVVAD).
Reasonably thorough ablations (Table 4) isolate contributions of dynamic video synthesis, contrastive negative-mining loss, and the language-guidance branch itself.
The data curation pipeline (retrieval + MLLM/VLM/LLM based cleaning and annotation) is a scalable approach that could be reused by others.
weaknesses: The paper's central claim -- that the model can genuinely adapt to changed/flipped anomaly definitions (true concept drift) -- is only demonstrated with two cherry-picked qualitative examples (Fig. 7). There is no systematic quantitative benchmark that measures performance specifically under label-flip/definition-change scenarios, which is surprising given this is framed as the paper's core contribution and motivating problem.

The large performance gains over baselines are confounded by the much larger and more diverse PreVAD training set; the paper's own ablation (Sec 6.3, 'Dataset Effectiveness') shows that simply retraining VadCLIP on PreVAD accounts for a substantial fraction of the improvement, making it hard to disentangle whether gains come from the proposed paradigm/architecture or just from more/better data.

The theoretical formulation in Sec. 3 (conditioning Φ on both v and z to avoid concept drift) is a fairly generic and well-known strategy (conditioning on auxiliary context to handle non-stationary label distributions); its presentation as a 'pioneering' formulation of concept drift in VAD somewhat overstates the technical novelty.

'Zero-shot' evaluation prompts are manually designed based on the target dataset's known class names, which is a weaker test of open-world, user-driven natural-language definition than the paper's motivating scenarios (e.g., hospital mask-wearing policy) would suggest; there's no evaluation with genuinely novel, user-authored natural language definitions beyond class names/descriptions already seen in training-like format.

Reproducibility concerns: the data curation pipeline depends on specific (and seemingly proprietary/unspecified in the main text) MLLM/VLM/LLM combinations for cleaning and annotation; dataset and code are only promised for future release, and annotation quality/noise from automated pipelines is not rigorously quantified (e.g., no measurement of description hallucination rate or annotation agreement with humans).

Baseline comparisons in Table 2 mix numbers taken directly from other papers with self-reproduced results, and training sets differ across rows (UCF, XD, PreVAD, AIGC+XD, etc.), making some of the headline comparisons (e.g., 'X% improvement') less rigorous/apples-to-apples than presented.

The architecture itself (CLIP encoder + temporal transformer + fusion + MIL losses) is largely a straightforward combination of existing components (similar to VadCLIP/OVVAD) with two added regularization losses; the individual technical novelty of dynamic video synthesis and hard-negative mining is incremental relative to prior data augmentation and contrastive learning literature.

No analysis of failure cases, computational cost, or sensitivity to the phrasing/quality of user-provided textual definitions, which is important given the method's practical claim of being usable by 'ordinary' users typing arbitrary language definitions at inference time.

strengths: Clearly motivated and formalized new problem setting (concept drift in VAD) with a principled probabilistic framing (Eq. 1-4) that distinguishes it from prior closed-set/open-set/open-vocabulary VAD paradigms.

PreVAD is a substantial dataset contribution: at 35,279 videos it is significantly larger and more diverse in domain coverage than existing VAD datasets, and uniquely provides multi-level category taxonomy plus fine-grained anomaly descriptions rather than just category labels, filling a real gap identified in Table 1.

Extensive zero-shot evaluation across seven diverse benchmark datasets (UCF-Crime, XD-Violence, MSAD, UBNormal, DoTA, TAD, LAD) with both detection (AUC/AP) and classification (Acc/F1) metrics, which is more comprehensive than prior open-world VAD papers.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of dynamic video synthesis, contrastive negative mining, and language guidance (Table 4), plus dataset-effect and architecture-effect analyses (Sec 6.3) that help attribute gains to specific design choices.

Qualitative case studies (Fig. 7) directly and intuitively illustrate the claimed capability of adapting to concept drift (redefining previously seen categories as normal/abnormal), which is a compelling demonstration of the paper's central claim.

The scalable, largely automated data curation pipeline (MLLM/VLM/LLM-based cleaning and annotation) is a practical contribution that could be reused/extended by the community for future dataset construction.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty of the model is somewhat incremental: dynamic video synthesis is an adaptation of existing Mosaic/Cutout-style augmentation, and the contrastive negative-mining loss is a fairly standard vision-language alignment technique; the main innovation lies more in the dataset and problem framing than in the model architecture.

No human evaluation or quality-control statistics are provided for the automatically generated anomaly descriptions and category labels in PreVAD (e.g., annotator agreement, sampled accuracy of MLLM-generated descriptions verified by humans), which is important given the dataset's automated pipeline and its central role in enabling the new paradigm.

The comparison with OVVAD (Table 2) is limited to only two datasets (UCF and XD) due to unspecified constraints, which weakens the strength of the central SOTA claim against the most directly comparable open-vocabulary baseline.

Classification metric definitions and comparison protocols shift across tables/baselines (e.g., some methods use ground-truth segments, others do not; F1 vs Acc trends are sometimes inconsistent, e.g., VadCLIP has higher F1 than LaGoVAD on UCF in Table 3 despite lower accuracy), which is not deeply discussed and could obscure genuine capability differences.

The paper does not report inference-time cost or practical usability trade-offs of requiring the fusion/language-conditioning branch at test time, which matters for a system intended for real-world open-world deployment.

Some baseline training-set mismatches (e.g., PEL/VadCLIP trained on UCF or XD vs. LaGoVAD trained on the much larger, more diverse PreVAD) make head-to-head SOTA claims partly attributable to dataset scale rather than purely to the proposed architecture/paradigm; while the paper partially addresses this via the 'dataset effectiveness' ablation, a fully controlled comparison (e.g., training baselines on PreVAD with their exact original architectures across all seven test sets) would strengthen the claims further.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and clearly formalized problem: concept drift in open-world VAD, distinguishing it from prior open-set/open-vocabulary/domain-generalization paradigms that assume fixed anomaly definitions.

Constructs PreVAD, a large-scale (35,279 videos, 209.5 hours) and diverse pretraining dataset with a hierarchical taxonomy (7 top-level, 35 sub-categories) and fine-grained anomaly descriptions, filling a real gap since most existing VAD datasets lack semantic descriptions.

Proposes a reasonably scalable and largely automated data curation pipeline (retrieval + MLLM/VLM/LLM-based cleansing and annotation) that could be reused by the community, with reported cost/quality tradeoffs.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across seven zero-shot test datasets (Protocol 1) plus a dedicated concept-drift evaluation (Protocol 2), with comparisons against a wide range of baselines (traditional, scene-dependent, open-vocabulary, domain-generalization, LLM-based).

Reasonably thorough ablations (loss components, language guidance, prompting strategies, synthesis hyperparameters, data scale) and qualitative visualizations that support the claimed benefits of dynamic video synthesis and negative-mining contrastive loss.

Consistent and often substantial performance gains over strong baselines (e.g., VadCLIP, PEL, LAVAD, Qwen2.5-VL) in both detection and classification metrics, as well as under simulated concept drift.
weaknesses: The core theoretical formulation (modeling Y as conditioned on both V and Z to avoid concept drift) is a relatively straightforward reformulation/conditioning trick rather than a deep methodological innovation; the architecture itself (CLIP encoders + Transformer fusion + MIL losses) is fairly standard, with novelty concentrated mainly in two auxiliary losses and the dataset.

Protocol 2, which is central to validating the paper's main claimed contribution (robustness to concept drift), is evaluated on only two datasets (XD-Violence, MSAD) with a small number of manually constructed category-subset 'definitions' (5 per dataset), which may not convincingly generalize to the richer, more subjective real-world concept drift scenarios motivating the paper (e.g., cultural/policy-based redefinitions).

PreVAD's annotation pipeline relies heavily on automated LLM/MLLM/VLM stages (captioning, consistency verification, abnormality judgment) with only partial human oversight (category labeling, frame-level labels for validation only); no inter-annotator agreement or systematic human quality audit of the generated descriptions is reported, raising concerns about label/description noise and hallucination despite claimed filtering steps.

Several baseline comparisons in Table 2 have missing entries (dashes) for many method/dataset combinations, likely due to lack of released code/checkpoints, which limits the completeness and fairness of head-to-head comparisons across all seven test sets.
The dataset and code are not available at submission/review time ('will be released'), limiting reproducibility and independent verification of the claimed scale/diversity/quality advantages.

Sourcing includes copyrighted/publicly scraped web videos (YouTube, streaming, traffic cameras); while the paper states there are no privacy/ethical issues, the risk of using web-scraped accident/violence compilation videos for a released research dataset (redistribution, consent, sensitive content) is not deeply addressed beyond a brief statement.

The comparison protocol for LLM-based methods (converting boundary predictions to binary frame scores) and the general fairness/tuning of baselines (e.g., prompt design) could bias results in favor of the proposed method, which is not fully controlled for.

strengths: Introduces a clear formalization of the 'concept drift' problem in VAD using a probabilistic framing (P(Y|V,Z)), which gives the paper a principled narrative for motivating language-conditioned detection.

Constructs a large-scale dataset (PreVAD) with 35K videos, a 7/35-level taxonomy, and free-form anomaly descriptions, which is a genuinely useful resource if released, and a reasonably detailed automated+human curation pipeline is described.

Extensive empirical evaluation across seven zero-shot test sets and two protocols (cross-domain and concept-drift-specific), along with fairly thorough ablations (dynamic synthesis hyperparameters, prompting strategies, data scaling, loss components).

Reasonable engineering combination of MIL-based binary detection, multi-class alignment, dynamic video synthesis for duration diversity, and contrastive hard-negative mining, with qualitative visualizations supporting the claimed benefits.
weaknesses: The core novelty claim is weaker than presented: open-vocabulary/CLIP-based methods (VadCLIP, OVVAD) already condition on text at inference and could, in principle, be re-prompted with new category definitions to handle drift; the paper's argument that these methods 'assume a fixed category set' is partly a framing choice rather than an inherent architectural limitation, so the distinction between the proposed paradigm and existing open-vocabulary VAD is less fundamental than argued.

The regularization techniques (MIL loss variants, contrastive learning with hard negative mining, synthetic video concatenation for duration diversity) are largely standard ideas from prior weakly-supervised VAD and contrastive learning literature repackaged for this setting, with limited genuinely new technical contribution; the paper itself acknowledges the architecture is 'simplified' and defers real architectural innovation to future work.

PreVAD's headline scale (35,279 videos) is inflated by including large portions of existing normal video-text datasets (VIDAL-10M, MSR-VTT, VATEX, VALOR account for ~57% of sources); the actual novel abnormal-video contribution (11,979 abnormal videos) is more modest and not dramatically larger than several existing datasets once normal filler data is excluded.

Dataset quality control relies heavily on multiple LLM/MLLM stages (captioning, matching, abnormality judging, description generation) with only spot human annotation on the validation set; no systematic human quality audit (e.g., precision/recall of the automated cleaning stages, description accuracy rates) is reported, leaving open concerns about label noise and hallucinated descriptions.

For Protocol 2 (concept-drift evaluation), most baselines (Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, LAVAD, HolmesVAU) are not designed for this exact task and are retrofitted with prompts or heuristic score binarization, making the comparison potentially uneven; only 5 hand-picked category subsets per dataset are used, limiting the statistical robustness of the concept-drift robustness claims.

Several performance comparisons are apples-to-oranges: e.g., Table 2 compares OVVAD trained on 'AIGC+XD/UCF' to LaGoVAD trained on 'PreVAD+XD/UCF' with only single numbers reported per cell and no shared training-data control, making it hard to attribute gains to the proposed method versus the additional/different training data.

The theoretical assumption that Y is solely determined by (V,Z) is asserted without empirical validation (e.g., no experiments isolating whether the model actually learns a faithful mapping conditioned on z rather than shortcutting through dataset-specific biases); the qualitative concept-drift example (Fig. 4) is a single anecdote rather than systematic verification.

No discussion of ethical/bias concerns despite using large volumes of scraped 'fail'/accident-compilation and surveillance-style web videos, which is notable in a submission focused on real-world deployment (e.g., surveillance for user-defined anomalies) and could raise fairness or misuse concerns not addressed in the paper.

Some quantitative gains, especially in Protocol 2 (e.g., MSAD-drift AP: 0.401 vs. 0.343 for HolmesVAU) are relatively modest given the added complexity of the proposed pipeline and dataset, raising questions about the practical significance of the improvements relative to simpler baselines.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: explicitly modeling concept drift in VAD via P(Y|V,Z) rather than P(Y|V), providing a clean theoretical framing that distinguishes this work from open-set/open-vocabulary/domain-generalization VAD approaches that assume fixed definitions.

Substantial new dataset (PreVAD) that is significantly larger and more diverse than existing VAD datasets (35,279 videos, 209.5 hours, 7 coarse/35 fine-grained categories), with a scalable semi-automated curation pipeline (retrieval + MLLM captioning + VLM verification + LLM filtering + human annotation) and, notably, per-video anomaly descriptions rather than just category labels, enabling the language-guided paradigm.

Extensive empirical evaluation across two well-designed zero-shot protocols (cross-domain generalization on 7 datasets, and a dedicated concept-drift protocol with resampled category subsets), which directly targets the paper's central claim rather than relying on a single in-domain benchmark.

Reasonably comprehensive comparisons against multiple families of baselines (traditional weakly-supervised VAD, open-vocabulary, scene-dependent, multi-domain, zero-shot CLIP/VLM-based, and recent LLM-based/agentic video anomaly methods), and thorough ablations isolating the contribution of dynamic video synthesis, negative mining, language guidance, dataset scale, and prompt type.

Clear qualitative analysis (concept-drift visualization, multi-anomaly video with fine-grained classification head outputs) that supports the quantitative claims and illustrates practical behavior differences versus LLM-based competitors.
weaknesses: The model architecture is intentionally simplified (frozen CLIP encoders + shallow co-attention fusion + linear/conv heads); the core technical novelty largely rests on two regularization losses and dataset construction rather than a fundamentally new architecture, which somewhat limits the technical contribution relative to the ambitious paradigm framing.

Dataset quality relies heavily on automated MLLM/LLM pipelines for description generation and abnormality judging; while some verification steps are included, there is no reported human evaluation of description accuracy/fidelity (only segment-level annotator agreement for the validation set is discussed), leaving open questions about label/description noise at scale.

The concept-drift evaluation (Protocol 2) is conducted on only two datasets (XD-Violence, MSAD) with 5 sampled subsets each, which is a fairly narrow empirical base for validating the paper's central claim about robustness to concept drift.

Some baseline comparisons rely on numbers taken directly from other papers (marked with † or ‡) trained/tested under different conditions (e.g., OVVAD only compared on 1-2 datasets rather than the full suite), making certain cross-method comparisons less apples-to-apples than the in-house reproduced comparisons.

The paper acknowledges the classification comparison setup favors baselines like CLIP/ActionCLIP/ViFi-CLIP (since they don't require temporal localization), and no variance/multiple-run statistics are reported for any table, making it hard to assess the robustness of the reported margins.

The theoretical claim that the definition Z could be images, video, audio, or learned embeddings is asserted but never empirically explored, so the generality of the paradigm beyond text is unverified.
